mu-7f1b30cb.stem: What is the order of structures in the femoral triangle from lateral to medial?
options: Femoral nerve, femoral artery, femoral vein, femoral canal
Femoral nerve, femoral vein, femoral artery, femoral canal
Femoral canal, femoral vein, femoral artery, femoral nerve
Femoral vein, femoral artery, femoral nerve, femoral canal
Femoral artery, femoral nerve, femoral vein, femoral canal
mu-7f1b30cb.explanation: From lateral to medial, 'NAVEL': nerve, artery, vein, empty space (femoral canal) and lymphatics. The femoral sheath encloses the artery, vein and canal; the nerve lies outside the sheath. A femoral hernia passes through the femoral canal and lies medial to the vein.

mu-16cc84f5.stem: After pelvic surgery a patient has sensory loss over the middle of the medial thigh, has difficulty crossing the legs, and swings the leg outwards when walking. Which nerve has been damaged?
options: Obturator nerve
Superior gluteal nerve
Sciatic nerve
Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve
Femoral nerve
mu-16cc84f5.explanation: The obturator nerve runs on the lateral pelvic wall, close to the ovary and the pelvic lymph nodes; it leaves through the obturator canal and supplies the adductor muscles and part of the skin of the medial thigh. When it is damaged adduction is weak and the leg swings outwards during walking.
notes: It supplies gluteus medius and minimus; its injury causes a Trendelenburg gait.
It supplies the hamstrings and everything below the knee.
It carries only sensation from the lateral thigh.
It supplies quadriceps and the front of the thigh.

mu-bbd5f796.stem: Which muscles insert into the iliotibial tract?
options: Sartorius and rectus femoris
Tensor fasciae latae and gluteus maximus
Biceps femoris and vastus lateralis
Piriformis and obturator internus
Gluteus medius and gluteus minimus
mu-bbd5f796.explanation: The iliotibial band is a thickening of the fascia lata on the lateral side of the thigh; above, TFL and the superficial fibres of gluteus maximus join it, and below it attaches to Gerdy's tubercle of the tibia. It stabilises the lateral side of the knee and the hip during standing.

mu-f83e1e4c.stem: Where is pain most often felt in iliotibial band friction syndrome?
options: Over the tibial tuberosity
Over the lateral epicondyle of the femur, on the lateral side of the knee
Over the pes anserinus
At the lower pole of the patella
Over the greater trochanter
mu-f83e1e4c.explanation: In runners, with the knee at 20–30° of flexion the band slides back and forth over the lateral epicondyle, and repeated friction causes pain on the lateral side of the knee. Pes anserinus bursitis causes pain medially, Osgood–Schlatter disease at the tibial tuberosity and jumper's knee at the lower pole of the patella.

mu-f2a216f9.stem: What is the order of structures in the popliteal fossa from superficial to deep?
options: Popliteal vein – tibial nerve – popliteal artery
Popliteal artery – tibial nerve – popliteal vein
Tibial nerve – popliteal vein – popliteal artery
Tibial nerve – popliteal artery – popliteal vein
Popliteal artery – popliteal vein – tibial nerve
mu-f2a216f9.explanation: In the popliteal fossa the tibial nerve is most superficial, the popliteal vein lies deep to it, and the popliteal artery is deepest and closest to the femur. That is why the artery is most at risk in supracondylar fractures of the femur.

options: From the medial condyle of the femur
From the head of the fibula
From the soleal line of the tibia
From the lateral surface of the lateral femoral condyle (and the lateral meniscus)
From the lower pole of the patella
mu-0ef3df79.explanation: The popliteus tendon passes inside the joint capsule to attach to the lateral femoral condyle; the muscle attaches to the posterior surface of the tibia above the soleal line. It unlocks the knee from full extension by rotating the femur laterally, and pulls the lateral meniscus backwards so that it is not trapped.

mu-7f7c1bd3.stem: Which muscle is the strongest invertor of the foot and dynamically supports the medial longitudinal arch?
options: Extensor hallucis longus
Flexor hallucis longus
Tibialis posterior
Fibularis longus
Tibialis anterior
mu-7f7c1bd3.explanation: The tibialis posterior tendon passes behind the medial malleolus and fans out to the navicular tuberosity and the plantar surfaces of the other tarsal bones. Tendon dysfunction is the commonest cause of acquired flatfoot in adults; the patient cannot rise onto the toes on one foot.

mu-f3d7394c.stem: Where does the fibularis longus tendon insert in the sole of the foot?
options: Into the navicular tuberosity
Into the medial cuneiform and the base of the 1st metatarsal
Into the tuberosity of the 5th metatarsal
Into the base of the 2nd metatarsal
Into the lateral surface of the cuboid
mu-f3d7394c.explanation: The fibularis longus tendon passes behind the lateral malleolus, then through the plantar groove of the cuboid, crossing the sole to reach the medial side; it plantarflexes and everts the foot and supports the transverse arch. Fibularis brevis inserts into the tuberosity of the 5th metatarsal.
notes: This is the main insertion of tibialis posterior.
This is the insertion of fibularis brevis.
This is not an insertion of this muscle.
The tendon passes through the groove under the cuboid; it does not attach there.

mu-5b4e4f42.stem: Which pair of tendons supports the foot from below like a 'stirrup'?
options: Tibialis anterior and fibularis longus
Tibialis posterior and flexor hallucis longus
Gastrocnemius and soleus
Extensor digitorum longus and extensor hallucis longus
Fibularis brevis and fibularis tertius
mu-5b4e4f42.explanation: Tibialis anterior from the medial side and fibularis longus from the lateral side both attach to the medial cuneiform and the base of the 1st metatarsal; together the two tendons form a stirrup under the foot that suspends the transverse and medial arches and balances inversion and eversion.

mu-04827f56.stem: Which statement about soleus is true?
options: It dorsiflexes the foot
It crosses both the knee and ankle joints
It arises from the femoral condyles
It is the main plantarflexor of the ankle when the knee is flexed
It is supplied by the deep fibular nerve
mu-04827f56.explanation: Soleus arises from the tibia and fibula and crosses only the ankle. When the knee is flexed, gastrocnemius is slack, so plantarflexion is produced mainly by soleus; as a postural muscle it works continuously during standing, and it is supplied by the tibial nerve.

mu-72bf97af.stem: A patient describes burning and numbness on the medial side of the heel and in the sole after long runs; percussion behind and below the medial malleolus produces paraesthesia. Which nerve is compressed?
options: Sural nerve
Tibial nerve
Superficial fibular nerve
Deep fibular nerve
Saphenous nerve
mu-72bf97af.explanation: In tarsal tunnel syndrome the tibial nerve or its plantar branches are compressed beneath the flexor retinaculum between the medial malleolus and the calcaneus, causing sensory disturbance in the sole and weakness of the intrinsic muscles. In the anterior tarsal tunnel the deep fibular nerve is compressed.

mu-0d6d2f9b.stem: Which structures are found in the second layer of the muscles of the sole?
options: Abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis and abductor digiti minimi
Quadratus plantae, the lumbricals and the FDL and FHL tendons
Quadratus plantae and abductor hallucis
Flexor hallucis brevis, adductor hallucis and flexor digiti minimi brevis
The interossei and the fibularis longus and tibialis posterior tendons
mu-0d6d2f9b.explanation: The four layers of the sole: 1) abductor hallucis, FDB, abductor digiti minimi; 2) quadratus plantae, the lumbricals, the FDL and FHL tendons; 3) FHB, adductor hallucis, FDMB; 4) the interossei with the fibularis longus and tibialis posterior tendons.
notes: These are two muscles from different layers.

mu-717fb0f4.stem: Through which toe does the axis of abduction–adduction of the toes pass?
options: The 1st toe
The 3rd toe
The 2nd toe
The 5th toe
The 4th toe
mu-717fb0f4.explanation: In the foot the dorsal interossei move the toes away from the axis of the 2nd toe and the plantar interossei bring them towards it. In the hand this axis is the 3rd finger.

mu-b3574b8e.stem: Where do the short extensor muscles on the dorsum of the foot arise?
options: From the lower end of the fibula
From the bases of the metatarsals
From the neck of the talus
From the navicular
From the superolateral surface of the calcaneus (in front of the sinus tarsi)
mu-b3574b8e.explanation: Extensor digitorum brevis and extensor hallucis brevis arise from the superolateral surface of the calcaneus; they are felt as a soft mass on the lateral side of the dorsum of the foot that can be mistaken for oedema or a lump. Both are supplied by the deep fibular nerve.
